[0:20:47] Thus P, although innocent in fact, must account for C's losses that were caused by A. This scheme is premised on the imposition of liability and the consequent obligation of compensation exclusively on the employer who in many cases may be completely innocent for employees' on-the-job injury, death, and loss of earnings,

[0:21:33] so-called losses. The enabling legislation for this system was a sort of social contract between the employer and the employee by which certain common law defenses which often operated as a de facto bar to the employer's liability and hence the employee's compensation for losses were eliminated in favor of the employers assuming any fact strict liability for all losses. As a result, responsibility for wrongs committed by employees is in many cases imputed exclusively to innocent employers who must bear the penalties for the wrongdoing of employees.

[0:22:24] Three, fidelity, performance, and related bonds or title insurance. Bonds are a widely used legal mechanism whereby party A as surety [snorts] guarantees to party C, the assured, the performance of an obligation of another party B, say a contractor. In the case of B's default, A will pay C for the losses resulting from B's wrongful non-performance. B's liability is thus imputed to A. Hence A, though innocent, bears the penalty of B, the actually guilty party.

[0:23:13] The bonding mechanisms are applied routinely in both civil and criminal contexts. Title insurance works similarly. A title company guarantees good title to an insured, a buyer, owner, or mortgagee. In the event of title failure, the title company will seek to cure the title, that is to remedy the defect at its own expense if it can, but if it cannot, it will pay a monetary penalty to the insured based on the proportion that the value of the loss bears to the insured value of the property.

[0:24:07] The liability of a guilty seller is thus imputed to the innocent title insurer who vicariously bears the penalty of the wrongdoer. Four, the law of indemnity.
